The researchers selected a virtual subsonic aircraft as the reference for this study.
A circular convergent nozzle was designed to meet the mission requirements of the virtual aircraft.
Various nozzle configurations were designed by changing the aspect ratio and curvature of the nozzle.
Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) analysis was used to study the thermal flow fields and nozzle surface temperature distributions.
A narrow-band model and the RadThermIR code were used to calculate the IR signatures of the plume and nozzle surface.
As the nozzle exit aspect ratio increased and the curvature increased, the IR signature of the plume and nozzle surface decreased.
The maximum reduction in IR signature for the non-circular nozzle configurations was 10.7% compared to the circular nozzle.
As the nozzle exit aspect ratio and curvature increased, the engine thrust decreased by up to 10.7%.
The researchers found that the changes in the temperature distribution and mixing with the surrounding air were the main factors contributing to the reduced IR signature.
The study highlights the trade-off between IR signature reduction and engine performance, suggesting the need for further optimization and integration of these factors.
The researchers used a compressible Navier-Stokes-Fourier CFD code to analyze the thermal flow fields and nozzle surface temperature distributions.
The narrow-band model used in the study considers the absorption and emission of radiation in specific wavelength bands.
The RadThermIR code is a widely used tool for calculating the infrared signatures of aerospace vehicles.
The researchers selected the nEUROn unmanned combat aerial vehicle (UCAV) as a reference for the nozzle design and analysis.
The mission profile of the virtual subsonic aircraft included takeoff, subsonic cruise, and high-speed cruise at an altitude of 36,000 feet.
